title: Binary Search: Find the First Yes

scenes.say: I'm thinking of a number from one to a million. You get twenty guesses. Sounds impossible? By the end, you'll win every time, and write the code with zero off by one bugs.

scenes.head: Every guess halves the range
scenes.say: Here's the trick. Guess the middle. Five hundred thousand? Too high, so half the numbers are gone. Guess the middle of what's left. Every guess halves the range, and a million shrinks to one number in twenty guesses. That halving is binary search.

scenes.head: First value at least 7
scenes.say: Sorted array. We want the first value at least seven. Lo starts at zero, and hi starts one past the end. The middle is index three, value seven. Big enough, so hi moves to three. The right half is out. Next middle is index one, value three. Too small, so lo jumps to two. Index two holds five. Still too small, so lo jumps again. Lo meets hi. The answer is index three.

scenes.head: The template that never goes off by one
scenes.say: Here it is in C plus plus. Lo and hi start at the two ends. While the range is not empty, take the middle. If the middle value is too small, the answer is to its right, so lo becomes mid plus one. Otherwise mid might be the answer, so hi becomes mid. When the loop ends, lo is the first index that is big enough. On our array it prints three.
Your turn. Same array, but search for eight. Which index comes back? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Three bugs interviewers watch for
scenes.say: It's five. Nine is the first value at least eight. Three classic bugs. Adding lo and hi can overflow, so add half the gap instead. Mixing two loop templates can loop forever, so pick one. And search for ten: lo ends at six, past the end. Check it before reading.

chapters.title: Search the answer, not the array

scenes.head: Smallest ship that works in 5 days
scenes.say: Now a problem with no sorted array at all. Ten packages weigh one to ten, and you have five days. What's the smallest ship that works? Ask a yes or no question for each capacity. Twelve: no. Thirteen: no. Fourteen: no. Fifteen: yes. Sixteen: yes. Once it says yes, it stays yes. So binary search for the first yes.
Quick one. If everything had to ship in one day, which capacity would the search return? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Weights 1 to 10, one day. Smallest capacity?

scenes.head: Binary search over capacities
scenes.say: Fifty five: the whole load in one trip. The smallest capacity is the heaviest package. The largest is the total. Check the middle. If it fits, try smaller. If not, go bigger. The check must never flip from yes back to no, or the search breaks. Here it returns fifteen.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does binary search work? Halve a range that holds the answer, every step. How fast? O of log n, so a million items take twenty steps. Search on the answer? Find the first yes of a check that never flips. Follow up: why lo plus half the gap? Lo plus hi can overflow.

scenes.say: Solve these three next. LeetCode thirty five, search insert position, is exactly today's lower bound. LeetCode thirty four, first and last position, runs it twice. LeetCode eight seventy five, Koko eating bananas, is search on the answer with a new check.

scenes.say: So say this. Binary search keeps a range that holds the answer and halves it. One template: lo less than hi, hi becomes mid, lo becomes mid plus one. And when a yes or no check never flips back, search the answer.
